messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

As she stood in her kitchen, expertly chopping vegetables for the evening's specials, Chef Alessia Bianchi couldn't shake the feeling of unease that had become all too familiar. It had been two years since her near-fatal bout with sepsis, a traumatic experience that had left an indelible mark on her life. The memory of those harrowing days in the ICU still felt like it was happening to her in vivid, Technicolor detail – the beeping machines, the antiseptic smell, the crushing pain. When these memories resurfaced, Alessia would often become overwhelmed with grief, feeling as though she was reliving the terror all over again. It was as if her body had developed a hair-trigger response to any perceived threat, reacting before her mind could even process what was happening. Alessia's partner, Rachel, had grown increasingly concerned about her withdrawal from social events and activities they used to enjoy together. Alessia would often excuse herself, citing exhaustion or stress, when in reality she was simply trying to avoid feeling anything too deeply. She had come to believe that her emotions were now permanently numbed, that she would never be able to feel normal again. This fear of emotional vulnerability led Alessia to employ a range of maladaptive strategies to cope with her distress. She would stay up until the early hours of the morning, replaying worst-case scenarios in her head, and avoid situations that might make her feel happy or hopeful – like meeting new people or trying new foods. It was as though she had lost trust in her own body, perceiving it as an enemy that was constantly on high alert, even when there was no real danger present. Alessia's perception of herself as physically vulnerable had become a self-fulfilling prophecy. Her hypervigilance made everyday situations feel fraught with peril – the sounds of sizzling meat in the kitchen would transport her back to the ICU, and the sight of a hospital on TV would send her heart racing. These reactions only reinforced her negative appraisals about her body's fragility, creating a vicious cycle that left her feeling trapped. One particularly disturbing flashback had occurred just last week while Alessia was preparing dinner at home. She had suddenly felt herself back in the ICU, surrounded by the sounds and smells of the hospital, and had become so overwhelmed that she had abandoned cooking altogether. This incident had shaken Rachel, who had urged Alessia to seek professional help. As Alessia reflected on her current state, she realized that her maladaptive strategies were only exacerbating her distress. She was now avoiding even the smallest pleasures in life – like trying new recipes or taking walks with Rachel – for fear of triggering another flashback. The memory of her traumatic experience had become so distorted and unreal that it felt like a perpetual shadow looming over her, always ready to pounce. What finally brought Alessia to seek help was the dawning realization that she couldn't keep living in this state of constant hypervigilance, numbing herself to the world around her. She longed to rediscover the joy and creativity that had once driven her passion for cooking – to feel normal again, without the weight of her traumatic experience constantly holding her back. As Alessia looked around her kitchen, she knew it was time to confront the fears and negative appraisals that had taken hold of her life. She hoped that with therapy, she could learn to rewire her responses, calm her body's alarms, and begin to heal – both physically and emotionally.
